claims.text: The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
A modified HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains 1 wt.% oxygen.
Experiments cover 0–200 K and 300–1200 K for both pure and 1 wt.% oxygen-doped samples.
The proposed approach will use an interatomic potential calibrated against ab initio data for pure and oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr.
The potential will explicitly represent oxygen-induced defect scattering within a conductivity-transport simulation.
Defect structures and oxygen-related scattering centers are relevant microstructural mediators in the alloy.
Defect and impurity scattering mechanisms dominate the electrical conductivity of the real alloy.
Perfect-crystal analytical models neglect the relevant defect and impurity scattering mechanisms.
Explicitly accounting for defects and oxygen impurities will make the simulated conductivity more accurate than conventional perfect-crystal analytical predictions.
The model will reproduce experimental conductivity within ±10% in both specified temperature regimes.
Existing defect-free analytical predictions typically deviate substantially when applied to materials containing impurities or defects.
The proposed applicability limit is 0–200 K and 300–1200 K for oxygen concentrations up to approximately 1 wt.%.
Performance outside the specified temperature ranges, above 1 wt.% oxygen, or for impurities other than oxygen is untested.
Prior work on Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni demonstrates that an HEA interatomic-potential/MD model can obtain quantitative agreement with first-principles calculations and experiments for structural properties.
A conductivity prediction for the 1 wt.% oxygen sample at 600 K that differs from the held-out measurement by more than 10% will falsify the hypothesis.
